A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching central formulations and theorem sequences. Their main texts, figures, equations, implementation table and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 Sections 5.3–5.5 and Figures 2–7 report original Gaussian and circular-data experiments, fairness–cost tradeoffs and inference-time measurements.

after.justification: v3 Section 5 and Appendix D report original synthetic and semi-synthetic dating experiments, held-out fairness measurements, discrete-matching experiments and solver-convergence results.

M1.justification: The core FairSinkhorn, penalized OT and bilevel formulations remain. v3 extends neural costs from a shared embedding to separate encoders for X and Y (Example 4.2), introduces learned feature-distance weights for dating data (D.3), and describes row-wise sampling for discrete matches (D.4). These are limited extensions within the existing framework.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only two-dimensional synthetic distributions. v3 adds a semi-synthetic dating task with compatibility restrictions and seven income groups (Section 5.2, D.3). It also replaces the three-group concentric-circle example with a two-group Gaussian-plus-circle scenario, materially changing represented data and matching conditions.

E2.justification: The relaxed-method comparisons remove ResNet cost learning and add vanilla entropic OT (v1 Figures 3/5; v3 Figure 3). Vanilla OT also becomes a held-out fairness comparator in v3 Figure 4; previously its reported comparison concerned exact versus penalized transport. Penalized OT, Mahalanobis and MLP comparisons remain.

E3.justification: v3 replaces the synthetic antidiagonal fairness target with [[0.20,0.30],[0.28,0.22]], changes the default synthetic epsilon from 2 to 1, and revises sample sizes, penalty grids and neural configurations. Table 1 raises the reported conditional-gradient iteration cap from 10 to 2000. KL-divergence utility evaluation is dropped, and new sampling and convergence protocols are introduced.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's geometry/model comparisons and reuse timing, v3 adds explicit training-versus-test fairness analysis (Figure 4), an entropy-sweep control (Figure 3c), sample-size-dependent fairness after discrete matching (D.4), and FairSinkhorn versus Sinkhorn convergence analysis (D.5). These substantially expand the practical and diagnostic questions tested.

E5.justification: Both versions report 10 runs for the reuse experiment. v3 adds test-fairness boxplots in Figure 4 and a separate 30-run averaging procedure with shaded bands for discrete matching in D.4/Figure 7b. The bands' statistical definition is unspecified; they are not identified as confidence intervals.

E6.justification: Under revised settings, v1's reported penalized-OT advantage on both synthetic datasets becomes similar Gaussian tradeoffs but superior penalized OT on Circles; v3 reports that Mahalanobis cannot reduce Circles fairness loss below 10^-2 (Figure 3). New results cover dating-task tradeoffs, training/test fairness gaps, discrete sampling and convergence. These additions and replacements do not establish same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The principal assumptions, existence/uniqueness result and Theorems 4.2/4.4 are retained with largely unchanged proofs. v3 C.2 adds a derivation of the sample-complexity constants' epsilon and lambda dependence, including exp(lambda Ks Kw/epsilon). v1 Appendix A's explicit FairSinkhorn convergence guarantee is removed; v3 instead reports empirical convergence.

C1.justification: The central contributions persist, but the cost-learning guarantee is moderated. v1's abstract describes a bound guaranteeing fair matchings from the learned cost on unseen data; v3 describes fairness deviation, and its contribution statement specifies finite-sample versus population deviation for costs in a parameterized family. This narrows the theoretical claim without changing the main theorem.

C2.justification: Section 4.3 changes an important interpretation: v1 calls cost learning more flexible, whereas v3 explains that parametric costs restrict attainable couplings and penalized OT is more flexible. v3 also clarifies the pointwise bound and adds specific limitations concerning individual fairness, downstream outcomes, normative target selection and simulated dating preferences (Conclusion, Impact Statement, D.3).

D1.justification: v1 promises future code release; v3 reports code availability and supplies repository access information. Appendix D adds initialization details and extensive dating-data filtering, compatibility, distance-construction and optimizer instructions. Some earlier neural-width and outer-iteration details are omitted, and v3 inconsistently reports 50 test Y samples in Section 5.1.4 versus 500 in D.2.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning relative to fairness-constrained bipartite matching and fair division (Section 2, Appendix A.2), including Castera et al. and Panda et al. It distinguishes feature-based representation, mass splitting and symmetry between populations. Structured-OT and inverse-OT references are also added, while much of v1's existing review is retained in Appendix A.

P1.justification: The main text is extensively condensed and rewritten. Related work is split between Section 2 and an extended appendix, and experiments are reorganized into synthetic and dating sections. v1's duplicate Approaches and Metrics subsections are removed; v3 adds dedicated limitations and impact discussions and revises the explanatory narrative.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main layout, redraws Figure 1 as a broader overview, and combines/redesigns the synthetic comparison plots. v1's individual transport-plan heatmaps are removed; v3 uses group-level mass insets and adds fairness boxplots, dating/compatibility figures and convergence/sampling panels. This is substantial visual reorganization.

improvement.justification: v3 addresses important empirical gaps in a paper previously evaluated only on two-dimensional synthetic problems. The dating experiment, entropy control, held-out fairness comparisons and discrete-sampling/convergence checks substantially strengthen support for practical claims. More calibrated theoretical wording, corrected method comparisons and expanded reproducibility information also improve quality. Missing implementation details and conflicting test-set sizes remain, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.
